After months of failed efforts to take Vicksburg by assaults from the north, by the early spring of 1863 Ulysses S. Grant had settled on a radically different approach. He would send a force over to the western bank of the Mississippi River; his troops would then march down through northern Louisiana, cross back over the river and establish a base of operations at Grand Gulf, Miss., about 30 miles south of Vicksburg, where there was less of a rebel presence. Grant could thus exploit advantageous terrain and weaker rebel defenses to move against the Confederate stronghold from the south.
To achieve his plan, Grant needed to divert Confederate attention and resources. So while he dealt with the huge logistical problems involved in an assault on Grand Gulf, Union forces engaged in a series of widespread but relatively small actions to keep John C. Pemberton, head of Confederate forces in Mississippi, from concentrating against Grant.
After a few weeks the stage was set for an even more ambitious endeavor in support of the Union assault: beginning on April 17, Col. Benjamin H. Grierson led a small contingent of troopers into northern Mississippi; 16 days and 600 miles later, Grierson and his men arrived exhausted but triumphant in Union-held Baton Rouge, La., having ridden the length of Mississippi. They had completed one of the most spectacular cavalry operations of the entire war.
Nothing in Grierson’s prewar life marked him as the man for this mission. Reared by abolitionist parents in Jacksonville, Ill., Grierson was a musical prodigy. He easily mastered many instruments, including the flute, clarinet, bugle, violin, guitar and piano. “I made music my profession for many years,” he recounted in his superb memoirs, “and was quite successful, having besides many pupils, numerous bands under my instruction throughout Ohio and Illinois.”
Library of Congress
Col. Benjamin Grierson, on the cover of Harper’s Weekly
When the war began, the 34-year-old Grierson was appointed to Benjamin H. Prentiss’s staff; by the spring of 1862 he was a colonel in the Sixth Illinois Cavalry. Although as a child he suffered facial disfigurement from a horse’s kick, there’s no evidence for the popular claim that Grierson was deathly afraid of horses; in fact, he seemed to master the cavalry arts as deftly as he did the musical ones. For several months Grierson served admirably in western Tennessee and northern Mississippi. William Tecumseh Sherman eventually reported to Grant that Grierson was “the best cavalry officer I have yet had.”
Grierson inspired this kind of confidence in all his superior officers. It’s a dubious distinction, though, to have been selected for an operation Grant and others were much less sure about. “The undertaking would be a hazardous one,” Grant wrote Stephen A. Hurlbut, Grierson’s commander as head of the XVI Corps, “but it would pay well if carried out.” Grierson recalled after the war that Hurlbut gave him only verbal orders because Hurlbut considered the mission too dangerous and doubtful “to take the responsibility to give definite or written orders for its execution.”
Nevertheless, in mid-April Grierson headed into Mississippi from the Union base at La Grange, Tenn. He had approximately 1,700 troopers, constituting three cavalry regiments — the    Sixth Illinois,  Seventh Illinois and    Second Iowa — as well as six small field guns. After a few days, Grierson had reduced his force by over a third, sending back to Tennessee some 200 riders unable to continue, along with the entire Iowa regiment.
Grierson’s remaining troopers, now totaling fewer than a thousand and utterly beyond the reach of Union aid, would wreak havoc across Mississippi over the next two weeks. They tore up miles of railroad, burned countless bridges and water towers and repeatedly cut telegraph communications across the state. As the raiders moved south they captured and paroled over a thousand Confederates, and they destroyed 500 stands of arms, dozens of rail cars, several thousand loaded shells and large amounts of food supplies (including 50,000 pounds of rebel bacon in a single day).
As Grierson explained after the war, the raid’s success flowed from a startlingly simple idea. “I considered what [the] rebel commanders would do as capable military men,” he wrote, “and what they would expect me to do. Then I did not do what was expected of me.”
Grierson thereby repeatedly duped Southern defenders. Early in his trek he sent out detachments to scatter tracking Confederate cavalry, creating the impression that he was merely making a foray into northern Mississippi. When he ordered soldiers back to La Grange, he directed them to spread widely so that citizens would report that his whole command had headed north. Late in the raid a captured Southerner was placed so as to overhear Grierson discussing false plans for moving his force. Then, as Grierson put it, the man was “slyly suffered to escape … that he might carry the information” back to the Confederate command. As a result, a superior rebel force waited for hours in an elaborate ambush attempt while the federals rode off in the opposite direction.
This was not the only time the Confederate defenders had no idea where Grierson was or where he was heading. On May 2, the same day Grierson jubilantly appeared in Baton Rouge, a Confederate captain near the Mississippi border reported that all he knew was that the Yankees had swept past his pickets and then disappeared. “I cannot learn where they came from,” he woefully stated, “or where they are at this time.” He was not alone in this confusion. Pemberton’s official report included the admission that “so great was the consternation created by this raid that it was impossible to obtain any reliable information of the enemy’s movements, rumor placing him in various places at the same time.”
But the Confederates didn’t merely not know where Grierson and his men were; they repeatedly failed to even realize who they were. The griminess of the long ride made it hard to recognize the federal blue worn by the troopers, and, in any event, Confederates regularly wore captured Union clothing. They blended in so well that one plantation owner upbraided Grierson’s men for riding quietly on remote back roads when they should instead be fighting Yankees. Another threatened to report the federals to Pemberton when they tied their horses to his trees. Grierson and his officers one morning were invited into still another plantation home, and enjoyed the charming hospitality of Mississippi women until a soldier blurted out something about Illinois cavalry. “The countenance of the hosts changed,” Grierson remembered, and he had to bid “the ladies good-bye rather hastily, and without waiting to finish the breakfast.”

In other instances, though, ignorance as to the federals’ identity is more understandable. Soon after slipping into Mississippi, Grierson decided to send out scouts dressed in Confederate butternut. This deception, under the laws of war, exposed soldiers to the death penalty if captured, so Grierson relied on volunteers, several of whom he would remember by name in his memoirs, written decades later.
By the time Grierson’s ride-wearied men stopped to briefly rest after crossing into Louisiana on May 2, Confederates were reporting that a force of up to 20,000 infantrymen and 6,000 cavalry had roared through Mississippi. So unexpected was Grierson’s achievement that when one of his orderlies fell asleep and rode all the way to the picket lines outside Baton Rouge, Union defenders thought his appearance was a trick to expose them to attack. Grierson appeared soon thereafter, but he still found it hard to convince his fellow Yankees “that we were really and truly ‘bona fide’ Illinois troops from Tennessee.”
Eventually, though, Grierson led his men through the streets of Baton Rouge, amid “the wildest shouts and cheers.” They rode on to a quiet magnolia grove beside the Mississippi River. There they would finally sleep “without guard and without danger.”
Grierson had done much more than display remarkable courage and daring. The raid snarled rebel communications, distracted the Confederate command and drew the attention of forces badly needed to defend against the Union threat growing on the Mississippi River’s western bank. In late April, after a naval assault against Grand Gulf that resulted in the fiercest river fighting of the war, Grant decided it wasn’t possible after all to land his forces there. Downstream from Grand Gulf, however, was an unimportant landing called Bruinsburg. On April 29, a Union patrol crossed the river and learned from a slave that the Confederate cavalry regiment that normally patrolled the area was gone.
The rebel cavalry had been sent away four days earlier in hopeless pursuit of Grierson. No Confederate troops were in the Bruinsburg area. When Grant subsequently learned that a road ran northeast from there, he knew he had his landing spot on the eastern bank of the Mississippi. The next day 24,000 Union soldiers and 60 guns moved across the river. It would take two more months to complete, but the final assault on Vicksburg had begun.
